10.1037/pspp0000619.title: Contextual predictors of state loneliness: The role of social company, activity, location, and duration of contextual exposure.
10.1037/pspp0000619.journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
10.1037/pspp0000619.abstract: Loneliness is not only a stable dispositional trait but also a momentary state that can fluctuate within individuals. However, empirical studies on how contextual factors relate to state loneliness remain scarce. This study investigated how state loneliness varies depending on social company, everyday activities, physical locations, and the duration of exposure to these contextual factors. Drawing on preregistered and exploratory analyses, we examined data from the Day Reconstruction Method module of the German Socio-Economic Panel Innovation Sample, collected across four waves between 2012 and 2015. The representative sample comprised 22,031 episodes nested within 2,508 participants (52.6% female, age range 17-95 years, M age = 50.0, SD age = 18.9). Multilevel logistic regression models showed that being alone consistently predicted higher odds of state loneliness, while the presence of others showed opposing associations. Participants were more likely to feel lonely when at home than when at work or elsewhere. Watching television was linked to a higher probability of reporting state loneliness, whereas self-care/health and media use showed a negative relationship. For some activities, this relationship was moderated by the duration of the activities: Reporting state loneliness was more likely during prolonged episodes of care work but less likely during prolonged episodes of social contact and television consumption. Overall, these findings contribute to a more robust, nuanced understanding of the contextual and temporal features tied to momentary feelings of loneliness, underscoring the need for dynamic, time-sensitive approaches in both research and interventions addressing everyday experiences of loneliness. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

10.1177/02654075261477595.title: Which Way Does Cupid’s Arrow Go? Distinguishing Happiness and Meaningfulness Within Romantic Relationships
10.1177/02654075261477595.journal: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
10.1177/02654075261477595.abstract: Happiness and meaningfulness are viewed as distinct aspects of psychological wellbeing, but their role in romantic relationships remains unknown. In two online studies, we sought to identify key differences between people’s judgments of relationship happiness and meaningfulness. Study 1 ( n = 426) found that greater sexual desire and satisfaction, and fewer relationship sacrifices and less stress, contributed to relationship happiness but were unconnected to relationship meaningfulness. By contrast, greater negative self-disclosure to one’s partner predicted relationship meaningfulness but was unlinked to relationship happiness. Study 2 ( n = 711) successfully replicated these findings, and further showed that people who prefer a meaningful relationship (over a happy one) exhibit a more favorable psychosocial profile, including greater relationship satisfaction, optimism, interpersonal closeness, forgiveness, and less relationship stress. These studies are the first to show that a distinct profile of psychosocial correlates distinguishes happy from meaningful romantic relationships, and they highlight the need for future research to consider hedonic and eudaimonic elements in relationship processes separately.

10.1177/01461672261481957.title: Is Authenticity Perceptible? Accuracy in Judgments of State Authenticity From Expressive Behavior
10.1177/01461672261481957.abstract: Substantial research provides evidence that being perceived as authentic benefits well-being and relationships, but under-examined is whether perceptions of authenticity are accurate. Across five studies, we tested whether perceivers can accurately discern others’ state authenticity. In Studies 1 to 3, we investigated correspondence between perceived and felt authenticity within acquainted dyads. Romantic partners accurately discerned each other’s authenticity after making sacrifices (Study 1) and after discussing a topic of personal distress and desired partner change (Study 2). However, partners failed to accurately perceive each other’s felt authenticity when discussing relationship conflict (Study 3), possibly impacted by cognitive or motivational processes elicited by the relatively high interpersonal stakes at play in conflict. In Studies 4A and 4B, outside observers were sensitive to authenticity differences in participants from Study 3 when watching thin-slice videos of the conflict conversations. Overall, we discuss the importance of authenticity for impression formation and close relationships.

10.1177/17456916261475589.title: Extending Truth-Default Theory to Misinformation: Connecting Misinformation Scholarship and Deception Research
10.1177/17456916261475589.abstract: This article connects deception research, specifically truth-default theory (TDT), to misinformation scholarship. Through TDT’s propositions and supporting empirics, we demonstrate how central questions in misinformation scholarship can benefit from deeper engagement with deception research and in particular TDT. Findings in the misinformation literature that have been surprising or unexpected (e.g., relatively few people are exposed to and share misinformation online) are predicted and explained by TDT. Robust conclusions from TDT about deception in human communication (e.g., people are truth-biased) are challenged by findings from misinformation research, prompting deeper investigation. Deception-detection research paradigms provide conceptual and empirical reference points relevant to the design of misinformation-detection tasks and interpretation of their results (e.g., true–false base rates, prompted vs. unprompted veracity judgments). Analytic approaches from TDT (e.g., analyzing accuracy for truthful and deceptive messages independently) support existing misinformation research aiming to understand the detection of misinformation and can holistically evaluate the outcomes of misinformation interventions, and TDT’s findings on how to improve deception-detection accuracy also suggest strategies for interventions that improve the detection of misinformation without undermining trust in credible news and information.

10.1177/02654075261498961.title: Self-Esteem as a Shared Resource Beyond Romantic Relationships: An Extension Into Friendships and Parental Relationships
10.1177/02654075261498961.journal: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
10.1177/02654075261498961.abstract: Self-esteem is an important factor in understanding relationship quality, for both the individual and their romantic partner. Yet, most research has focused on solely romantic relationships, neglecting other close relationships that are at least equally important for understanding humans. In the present analysis, introductory psychology students at a Canadian university and their significant other (romantic partner, close friend, or primary caregiver) completed measures of self-esteem and relationship quality ( N = 308 dyads). Actor-Partner Interdependence Model analyses replicated and extended Robinson and Cameron’s (2012) findings that the higher dyad members’ combined self-esteem, the higher the dyad-level relationship quality. Thus, self-esteem may serve as a shared resource in romantic, friend, and family relationships.

10.1016/j.copsyc.2026.102474.title: Cross-cultural and Indigenous perspectives on music and social bonding
10.1016/j.copsyc.2026.102474.abstract: Experimental studies of primarily Western participants have suggested that musical synchrony facilitates social bonding. However, critics question the validity and cross-cultural generality of synchrony-bonding relationships, as well as the causal role of music. Drawing on recent data from large-scale Registered Reports co-designed and implemented with over 100 collaborators ("Many Voices"), we show that group singing enhances social bonding significantly more than speaking, across 901 participants speaking 30 languages. We share lessons from this collaboration regarding evolutionary hypotheses about the origins of music and language, as well as the importance of collaborating with Indigenous and non-Western researchers. By making the psychology of music research more inclusive, we may broaden our understanding of music and social bonding in humans and beyond. Indigenous knowledge does not oppose science: it improves science.

10.1177/02654075261496338.title: Lonely in Love, Driven to Buy: How Perceived Partner Materialism Influences Loneliness and Consumption in Romantic Relationships
10.1177/02654075261496338.journal: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
10.1177/02654075261496338.abstract: Loneliness is increasingly prevalent and carries significant consequences for well-being, yet it remains common even within romantic relationships. Drawing on Self-Determination Theory and the Discrepancy Model of Loneliness, this research conceptualizes loneliness as arising when relationships fail to satisfy individuals’ need for relatedness, resulting in perceived gaps in closeness. Moving beyond prior work on value congruence, this research examines how perceptions of a partner’s materialism are associated with loneliness, relational outcomes, and consumption behavior. Results from a survey study ( N = 546) indicate that both perceived partner materialism and personal materialism are associated with greater loneliness, suggesting that unmet expectations for closeness, not value similarity, are linked to this experience. In contrast, perceived partner materialism is related to higher relationship satisfaction only among individuals who are themselves more materialistic. Perceived partner materialism and loneliness are also associated with compulsive buying and product retention tendency, even after controlling for personal materialism. Together, the findings highlight the role of perceived partner values in shaping both relationship experiences and consumer responses to unmet relational needs.

10.1037/pspp0000616.title: The temporal dynamics of narcissism and aggression: Timescales, moderators, and generalizations in diverse samples.
10.1037/pspp0000616.journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
10.1037/pspp0000616.abstract: The relationship between narcissism and aggression has received considerable research attention, with the main conclusion being that individuals with higher levels of narcissism tend to exhibit more aggressive behavior. However, most evidence comes from cross-sectional and experimental studies using between-person analyses and relies heavily on Western convenience samples, leaving the temporal dynamics and within-person processes largely unexplored. This preregistered study examined four large-scale data sets of Chinese undergraduates and offenders: two ambulatory assessment samples (427 undergraduates and 775 offenders; 19,331 and 42,820 observations, respectively) and two long-term longitudinal samples ( N = 1,404, 969, 822, 613 for undergraduates and 2,064, 1,716, 1,609, 1,393 for offenders, each with four assessments over a year). Results indicated that narcissism and aggression prospectively predicted one another at the momentary level, but not the long-term level. These reciprocal effects were largely replicated across undergraduate and offender samples. Person-level narcissism and aggression moderated several of these dynamic associations, with the most robust pattern showing that higher person-level aggression consistently strengthened the effects of narcissistic states on subsequent aggression among offenders. Overall, this study provides, to our knowledge, the first within-person evidence for dynamic reciprocal associations between narcissism and aggression, while also offering stronger support for the robustness, cultural generalizability, and population representativeness of these processes. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

10.1177/01461672261485365.title: Grateful for What and Whom? How Gratitude List Content Varies and Is Associated With Affective Responses
10.1177/01461672261485365.abstract: A gratitude list activity, whereby one recalls and writes down things they are grateful for, is a well-studied intervention known to confer an immediate and even prolonged boost in well-being. However, the specific content people reflect on, and how it relates to affective evaluations and the impact of the intervention, remains underexplored. Using data from a global online study ( N = 19,265), we applied natural language processing to examine the content of gratitude lists, identifying 16 thematic clusters, with the most common one focused on social relationships. Next, we examined and found various sociodemographic and psychological differences in people’s gratitude list content. Further, mentioning themes related to family or nature was associated with greater increases in positivity following the activity. Overall, our findings highlight individual differences in what people naturally think of during this popular intervention and suggest opportunities for personalized modifications to enhance adherence to and effectiveness of the intervention.

10.1177/17456916261479948.title: How Sexually Objectifying Others Undermines Connection and Collaboration
10.1177/17456916261479948.abstract: Sexual objectification is widely recognized as a driver of gender inequality, harming women by reducing them to bodies and undermining their agency. Yet psychological science has rarely asked a consequential question: Does sexual objectification also harm the individuals who objectify? In this theoretical article, we reframe objectification as not only oppressive but also self-undermining. Drawing from social, cognitive, organizational, and relationship science, we argue that objectifying others can compromise the capacity to form close relationships, collaborate effectively, and function well in social and professional life. These costs are traced to four mechanisms—cognitive load, face–body attentional trade-off, goal-based perception, and dehumanization. These mechanisms are proposed to operate as parallel, mutually reinforcing pathways that converge on social miscalibration. The framework further motivates a methodological agenda for studying objectification as a dynamic, dyadic process embedded in ongoing interaction. By foregrounding the objectifiers’ costs, we extend existing theories and highlight objectification as a mode of social perception that degrades the very relationships and institutions on which objectifiers rely. Identifying these costs offers an additional reason to reduce objectification, one that complements rather than replaces concern for the harms it inflicts on targets.

10.1111/pere.70091.title: Validation of the Marital Offense‐Specific Forgiveness Scale ( MOFS ): Invariance Measurement Across Christian and Muslim Couples in Germany
10.1111/pere.70091.abstract: Forgiveness is a critical factor in marital stability and satisfaction, particularly within religiously diverse societies where interpretations of relational offenses may differ. This study assessed the measurement invariance of the Marital Offense‐Specific Forgiveness Scale (MOFS) across Muslim and Christian adults in Germany. A total of 935 participants (287 Muslims, 648 Christians) were recruited from Catholic and Muslim congregations in Germany through convenience sampling. Multi‐group confirmatory factor analysis supported the two‐factor structure of the MOFS—Benevolence and Resentment/Avoidance—and demonstrated configural, metric, and partial scalar invariance, enabling meaningful cross‐group comparisons. Full scalar and residual invariance were not established. Latent mean analyses revealed significantly higher resentment/avoidance among Christian participants, with no significant group differences in Benevolence. These findings support the cross‐religious validity of the MOFS and underscore the role of cultural and religious contexts in shaping emotional responses to marital offenses. Clinical implications for interventions with interfaith couples are discussed, and future research directions include the exploration of additional cultural factors and the use of longitudinal designs.

10.1177/17456916261482033.title: Two Practices That Understate the Mental Health Risks Associated With Adolescent Social-Media Use
10.1177/17456916261482033.abstract: Why do researchers analyzing the same body of evidence reach different conclusions about whether social-media use poses risks to adolescent mental health? We offer a partial explanation: Two common practices can lead researchers to underestimate harm and reach divergent conclusions. First, studies often do not account for risk elevations, relying instead only on correlation coefficients, which are more prone to misinterpretation. Second, researchers often rely on highly blended analyses that combine heterogeneous exposures (e.g., multiple digital activities, including “TV watching”), outcomes (e.g., depression with life satisfaction), and populations (e.g., girls with boys), and then treat weak aggregate associations as evidence that specific risks are negligible. This is especially problematic when the central question is whether heavy social-media use is associated with internalizing symptoms among adolescent girls. We illustrate how sequential blending can transform a large and clinically relevant association into a negligible one, which helps explain the persistent disagreement in the literature. We conclude by urging researchers to present their findings in more practically interpretable terms, including elevated risks, and to investigate heterogeneity across platforms, usage levels, populations, and outcomes.

10.1146/annurev-psych-020226-033620.title: Toward a Unified Theory of Group Connection
10.1146/annurev-psych-020226-033620.abstract: Behavioral scientists have long been struck by the human tendency to connect with other individuals and groups. Three major approaches to group connection have been advanced: ( a ) the social cohesion approach, ( b ) the social identity approach, and ( c ) identity fusion theory. While each approach has garnered support, no one has attempted to integrate them. We address the need for integration by proposing a general theoretical framework that specifies the unique contributions of each approach, identifies the psychological phenomena each best explains, and reconciles theoretical inconsistencies. We then propose a network model that spells out how different aspects of the self-concept, in accordance with key insights from the three approaches, engender group connection.

10.1177/02654075261496954.title: Associations Between Adult Attachment and Social Anxiety in Romantic Partner Situations: Does Perceived Dyadic Coping Play a Mediational Role?
10.1177/02654075261496954.journal: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
10.1177/02654075261496954.abstract: Adult attachment anxiety and attachment avoidance are associated with negative individual and relational outcomes. However, it is unknown whether these insecure attachment styles are associated with social anxiety in romantic partner situations, and whether dyadic coping may play a mediating role in these associations. The current study tested these possibilities. A community sample of adults who reported being in a romantic relationship ( N = 88) completed measures of adult attachment, dyadic coping style of their partner, and a newly developed measure of social anxiety for romantic partner situations. Attachment anxiety and attachment avoidance were significantly and positively associated with social anxiety in romantic partner situations. Perceived negative dyadic coping partially mediated these associations, whereas perceived supportive dyadic coping did not mediate these associations. These findings suggest that an individual’s insecure attachment style is associated with higher social anxiety levels in relation to their romantic partner, and this association is in part accounted for by the perception of negative dyadic coping of the partner in response to stressors within the relationship. The findings also highlight the importance of relationship-based mediators in explaining links between insecure adult attachment styles and their outcomes.

10.1037/apl0001420.title: A meta-analytic examination of the criterion-related validity and cognitive loading associated with traditional and new situational judgment test paradigms.
10.1037/apl0001420.abstract: Traditionally, situational judgment tests (SJTs) include text-based situations and ask candidates to pick the best and worst response option. Over the years, various new SJT paradigms have been developed to increase validity, reduce incidental cognitive load, and/or lower costs. Examples are multimedia SJTs, constructed response SJTs, and single-response SJTs. First, this study investigates how the traditional SJT paradigm performs in terms of criterion-related validity by updating prior meta-analyses. Second, this study provides initial, meta-analytic evidence on the criterion-related validity and cognitive load of several new SJT paradigms. On the basis of 457 independent samples from 302 studies (total N = 244,257), results showed that SJTs were not only predictive of job performance but also of academic performance, organizational citizenship behavior, and counterproductive work behavior. SJT validity was higher in operational (i.e., applicant) settings than in nonoperational settings and could also be expanded to new content (e.g., emotion and cross-cultural management). In terms of comparing traditional and new SJT paradigms, multimedia SJTs had validity equal to text-based ones but lower cognitive load. Importantly, the multiple-choice modality did not significantly outperform written constructed response modalities in terms of validity, and the cognitive loading of webcam-constructed responses was even lower than that of other response modalities. The implications of these findings are among others discussed in the context of the cost effectiveness of SJTs vis-à-vis other selection procedures. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

10.1037/apl0001425.title: Industrial-organizational science that matters: Social impact and policy implications in the Journal of Applied Psychology.
10.1037/apl0001425.abstract: This introductory article to the special issue "Social Impact Research" examines the extent to which research published in the Journal of Applied Psychology has addressed pressing social issues related to work and employment. Using BERTopic modeling on 5,865 empirical articles published from the journal's inception in 1917 through June 2024, we identified 99 topics organized into 25 higher order themes, five of which directly reflect social impact: workplace stress, health, and well-being; workplace diversity, equity, and inclusion; organizational justice, ethics, and legal issues; work and employment transitions across the lifespan; and social justice and labor opinions . Trend analyses from 1980 to 2024 revealed growth in health and well-being research, relatively stable publication of diversity, equity, and inclusion scholarship, an inverted-U trajectory for justice and legal topics, and the disappearance of labor-related research. We then introduce the 19 special issue articles (appearing in the October and November 2026 issues) which address employment barriers facing marginalized and economically disadvantaged workers, medical benefits and leave policies, gender and women's employment, and macrolevel societal disruptions, each offering actionable implications related to work that can benefit the greater good. We conclude by proposing a future social impact research agenda that suggests industrial-organizational (I-O) psychologists conduct research that addresses key issues such as economic insecurity, immigrant and refugee workers, generative artificial intelligence, climate change, and political instability. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

10.1016/j.jvb.2026.104297.title: Daily job crafting with generative artificial intelligence: Implications for work meaningfulness and engagement
10.1016/j.jvb.2026.104297.abstract: As Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen-AI) becomes embedded in daily work, understanding how employees proactively engage with these tools to shape their work experiences is increasingly important. Building on self-determination theory and the job crafting literature, this study introduces the concept of daily Gen-AI-driven job crafting: employees' self-initiated use of Gen-AI to modify their daily job demands and resources. We examine whether Gen-AI-driven job crafting is associated with daily work engagement through psychological need satisfaction and work meaningfulness. We employed a daily diary design with 149 UK-based full-time employees (M age = 36.7, SD age = 10.4; 63.8% male) who used Gen-AI at work daily or multiple times per day over ten consecutive workdays, incorporating a brief open-ended question to examine whether employees experienced their Gen-AI use as intentional work modification. Quantitative results showed that the dimensions of Gen-AI-driven job crafting (augmenting instrumental resources, augmenting social resources, augmenting challenging demands, and automating hindering demands) were differentially associated with daily work engagement through need satisfaction (autonomy, competence, relatedness) and, in turn, work meaningfulness: the competence pathway received the most consistent support, while the relatedness pathway was the most limited. Open-ended responses were consistent with intentional work modification, for instance, automating hindering demands was framed as a strategic reallocation of cognitive resources toward more valued work rather than simple workload reduction. Together, these findings suggest that Gen-AI may function as a bottom-up work design tool associated with daily need satisfaction and engagement.

10.1016/j.jvb.2026.104308.title: Are the basic psychological needs of self-determination theory necessary for employee well-being?
10.1016/j.jvb.2026.104308.abstract: The basic psychological needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness in self-determination theory (SDT) were originally defined and interpreted as necessary for well-being. Although this necessity assumption has been a cornerstone of SDT for over three decades, no systematic evidence has yet emerged to support it. This knowledge gap largely stems from a theory-method misfit. Most empirical studies use regression-based analytical techniques that do not align with necessity logic because they reflect a probabilistic “average-effect” logic. Necessary condition analysis (NCA) is an appropriate method specifically designed for identifying necessary conditions. In the present research, we adopt NCA to examine whether autonomy, competence, and relatedness are necessary for employee evaluative well-being (job satisfaction and work meaningfulness), affective well-being (positive affect), and conative well-being (work engagement). Across three studies, we found consistent support for the necessary role of psychological need satisfaction in all four well-being indicators, with nuanced variations in these necessity relationships. In contrast, power and status were not found to be necessary. These findings advance our understanding of basic psychological needs through a necessity-oriented lens and underscore the importance of fostering a need-supportive work environment in organizations.

10.1037/apl0001407.title: A meta-analysis of the dynamism of emergent states and team processes.
10.1037/apl0001407.abstract: Prevailing theories of teamwork propose that a team's cognitive, affective, and motivational states (i.e., emergent states) and its members' interdependent actions (i.e., team processes) are inherently dynamic. Nevertheless, much of the existing literature overlooks critical components of theories on system dynamics (e.g., inertia, coevolution, feedback) and has largely failed to consider how time operates, ultimately leading to a predominantly static view of teams. To extend our understanding of team dynamism, we synthesized over 3,000 correlation coefficients from longitudinal studies, representing more than 11,000 teams on average. Using cross-lagged, meta-analytic structural equation models, we found that (a) emergent states and team processes exhibit inertia over time, although this varies by construct (affect exhibits the least inertia, while conflict exhibits the most); (b) some constructs (team affect and team cognition) tend to coevolve with team processes over time, whereas others (team motivation and team conflict) are consistently predicted by earlier team processes; (c) team performance exhibits consistent feedback loops, predicting subsequent emergent states and processes, which, in turn, predict later performance; and (d) the length of time between observations moderates these dynamics. Drawing on these results, we outline several key theoretical considerations for understanding team dynamics, highlight important methodological considerations for conducting longitudinal causally identified teams research, and offer recommendations for advancing beyond the current static perspective to a more dynamic understanding of teams. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

10.1111/peps.70044.title: Personnel Psychology's 40 Questions Series: Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion in Organizations
10.1111/peps.70044.abstract: This article presents a curated set of 40 questions on diversity, equity, and inclusion in organizations (DEI) to address myths and misperceptions about its role in Industrial/Organizational (I/O) Psychology and Management research and practice. We crowdsourced questions from our professional networks and organized the responses into themes including foundations of DEI, the business case, DEI effectiveness, DEI resistance, legal interpretations, DEI pullback, measurement, and programs and vehicles. Though the review is not entirely comprehensive, the aim is to utilize the most up‐to‐date literature to answer many of the most pressing questions about DEI.

10.1146/annurev-psych-030226-025335.title: Psychology of Culture Change: The Power of Situations Returns
10.1146/annurev-psych-030226-025335.abstract: Creating inclusive cultures with equal opportunity and belonging is a goal of most communities and organizations, but achieving that goal has been uneven at best. Many attempts at inclusive culture change have not worked, while others have backfired. One reason is that these attempts have exclusively emphasized individual efforts and underestimated the power of situations in nudging individuals’ beliefs, behaviors, interactions, and relationships, which together create local culture. This article disaggregates the power of situations into four distinct types of situational forces, by integrating research from social psychology and adjacent disciplines, to illustrate how some situational forces shift beliefs, behaviors, social interactions, and relationships toward greater inclusion and equality while other situational forces move in the opposite direction. An important goal is to illuminate how individual beliefs and behaviors connect to higher-order changes in local cultures and to identify where research is lacking to chart a future research agenda.

10.1037/apl0001424.title: The shape of recovery activities: A person-centered study of evening recovery activity profiles, their work antecedents, and outcomes.
10.1037/apl0001424.abstract: Evening off-job activities play a crucial role in recovery from work. Although previous research has provided valuable insights into the role of recovery activities, little is known about the complex interplay of multiple characteristics of recovery activities and how this relates to well-being and work outcomes. Building on a dimensional approach to differentiate key characteristics of recovery activities (physical, social, creative, mental, spiritual, virtual, and outdoor), we adopt a person-centered perspective to identify distinct recovery activity profiles that capture the various ways these characteristics co-occur in daily life. We further investigate the extent to which these profiles shape recovery experiences, well-being, and work outcomes. Using data from two 10-day daily diary studies, Study 1 ( N = 345, 1,907 observations) identified daily profiles and demonstrated their associations with recovery experiences, emotional exhaustion, and next-morning vigor. In Study 2 ( N = 321, 1,780 observations), we assessed to what extent these profiles replicated in an independent sample and extended the investigation by including work-related antecedents and next-day work outcomes. Results indicated that daily recovery activities cluster together into identifiable profiles that largely replicated across samples. The identified profiles exhibited unique relationships with recovery experiences, well-being, and work outcomes. Our findings add to the recovery literature by illustrating the merits of considering profiles of recovery activities and their characteristics rather than studying recovery activities in isolation. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

10.1111/peps.70043.title: Closing the Gap, Carrying the Burden: How Gender and Prosocial Motivation Shape Workplace Recognition
10.1111/peps.70043.abstract: Despite progress toward gender equity, women remain disadvantaged in gaining workplace recognition. We theorize that prosocial motivation helps women achieve parity in workplace recognition by providing a role‐congruent path to becoming valued advice sources. Drawing on social role theory and role congruity theory, we propose that women are less likely than men to occupy central positions in advice networks, but that high prosocial motivation closes this gap. Advice centrality, in turn, functions as a peer‐conferred signal of workplace recognition that supports leadership emergence and performance ratings. Across a time‐lagged, multi‐source field study and two online experiments, we find support for this model. Study 1 ( n = 275) shows that women occupy less central positions in advice networks than men, but that high prosocial motivation closes this gap. Advice network centrality further mediates the interactive effects of gender and prosocial motivation on leadership emergence and performance ratings. Two online experiments (Study 2a, n = 247; Study 2b, n = 248) provide converging causal evidence for these effects. These findings show that prosocial motivation helps women achieve parity with men in workplace recognition, while raising the possibility that such parity may rest on demands that fall asymmetrically on women.

10.1111/peps.70041.title: The Bamboo Ceiling in the UK: Ethnicity–Gender Intersectionality, Risk Tolerance, and Leadership Attainment
10.1111/peps.70041.abstract: In the UK, Asians are often perceived as the “model minority” who face few hardships due to their strong educational performance and economic success. We question this perception by uncovering a “Bamboo Ceiling” in leadership attainment for certain Asian subgroups in the UK. Whereas many researchers and practitioners treat Asians as a monolith, we recognize heterogeneity among Asian subgroups and focus on comparing ethnic Chinese (the largest East Asian group) and ethnic Indians (the largest South Asian group). In Study 1, we analyzed CEOs and CFOs of the Financial Times Stock Exchange (FTSE) companies—the largest publicly listed companies in the UK—over a 14‐year period (2011–2024). There were virtually no ethnic Chinese CEOs or CFOs, whereas the representation of ethnic Indians in these positions did not differ significantly from that of Whites. In Study 2, we analyzed a large, nationwide dataset from the UK Biobank ( N = 322,734) to further investigate the moderating role of gender and the mediating role of risk tolerance. While ethnic Chinese overall experienced a Bamboo Ceiling (thus confirming Study 1's results), this main effect was moderated by gender: Ethnic Chinese men were significantly less likely than ethnic Indian and White men to attain leadership positions, a pattern partly mediated by ethnic differences in risk tolerance; by contrast, ethnic Chinese, Indian, and White women did not differ significantly and were each disadvantaged relative to their male counterparts. These effects were robust across survey‐based and polygenic measures of risk tolerance. Together, these findings underscore the importance of distinguishing among Asian subgroups and examining how ethnicity and gender intersect in leadership attainment.

10.1016/j.copsyc.2026.102468.title: Conflict expression: A decade of group conflict research
10.1016/j.copsyc.2026.102468.abstract: The conflict expression framework was developed to generate new practical and theoretical insights into how conflict communication affects group processes and negotiated outcomes. The framework proposes that conflict expressions vary along two dimensions: directness and oppositional intensity. The framework suggested that the effects of different types of conflict on group processes and outcomes likely depend on how the conflict is expressed, that conflict within groups is likely perceived differently by different members of the same social unit, and that conflict affects negotiation processes dynamically through reciprocated statements and responses. We review research building on the framework - including empirical tests of the main propositions, methodological advances, and as a theoretical foundation for conflict communication research more broadly - and identify directions for the future.

10.1146/annurev-psych-031626-100451.title: Consensus, Disagreements, and Open Questions in the Psychology of Misinformation
10.1146/annurev-psych-031626-100451.abstract: Research on misinformation has expanded rapidly over the past decade. This review examines areas of consensus and contention within the literature on misinformation, with particular attention to conceptual definitions, measurement approaches, and theoretical explanations. We outline views on what it means to be susceptible to misinformation and advocate for assessing susceptibility by focusing on the ability to discern true from false claims. Although exposure to fake news is less common online than many think, we argue that misinformation—more broadly construed—continues to be a major problem. We review evidence on cognitive and socio-affective mechanisms underlying susceptibility to misinformation, including repetition effects, lack of analytic reasoning, political identity, and information environments. We also evaluate interventions such as fact-checking, prebunking, psychological inoculation, and accuracy prompts. Overall, the literature reveals several robust findings but also significant methodological limitations and theoretical disagreements that suggest fruitful future directions for misinformation research.

10.1016/j.copsyc.2026.102453.title: Suppressed inquiry: The hidden toll of working with satisfaction-optimized AI
10.1016/j.copsyc.2026.102453.abstract: LLMs have become thinking companions for hundreds of millions worldwide, and they often do remarkable work. But their satisfaction-optimized design produces suppressed inquiry: the tendency for LLMs to inhibit rather than facilitate users' questioning process. LLMs appear fluent, confident, and seemingly all-knowing, their near-instant and polished output making non-LLM work feel unacceptably tedious and less eloquent. They affirm rather than interrogate users' assumptions, producing output that is deceptively adequate-shallower, less original, and less carefully reasoned than it appears. Seemingly competent systems also reduce vigilance and the monitoring impulse that independent judgment requires. Their responses also confine users within the frame they establish, narrowing what users think to ask. These costs are self-concealing: detecting them requires the very engagement that they suppress. And repeated delegation gradually atrophies users' capacity to reason independently. Three converging pressures make correction difficult: commercial incentives that reward satisfaction over substance, LLMs' tendency to revert to satisfaction-optimized defaults even when users push back, and a societal drift toward less-effortful engagement. We propose a research agenda to deepen the understanding of suppressed inquiry and how to counter it, to move closer to the remarkable thinking partners LLMs promised to be.

10.1111/peps.70046.title: Inclusive Leadership as a Site of Struggle: Resistance and Mitigation Strategies for Sustaining Inclusion for Historically Marginalized Employees
10.1111/peps.70046.abstract: Scholars emphasize inclusive leadership's benefits for leaders and employees, yet existing theory largely overlooks the challenges leaders face when addressing disparities experienced by historically marginalized employees. Drawing on an inductive study of 47 historically marginalized STEM employees and 14 leaders they identified as inclusive, we model inclusive leadership as a three‐part process: (1) leaders’ inclusion efforts (attentive learning, talent amplification, and structural debiasing); (2) resistance to these efforts (skepticism, gatekeeping, fit critiques, and non‐compliance); and (3) leader strategies to mitigate resistance and protect inclusion (explaining value, co‐crafting strategies, evaluating fit critiques, and managing change momentum). We triangulate findings and test our theory's boundary conditions using qualitative data from three additional STEM samples: racial minority men, lower‐ranking women, and White males. The first two samples replicate our model; the third reveals that White men may perceive inclusive leadership differently than historically marginalized employees. By centering the perspectives of those most affected by bias, our study extends inclusive leadership theory. We offer a processual view that moves beyond detailing inclusive behaviors to highlight the challenges leaders face enacting them.

10.1037/rev0000647.title: Why most stereotypes are negative.
10.1037/rev0000647.abstract: Stereotypes are a foundational construct in psychological science, often defined as beliefs concerning characteristic group attributes. We present a cognitive-ecological theory of social perception that predicts and explains why such characteristic attributes are likely negative, that is, why most stereotypes are negative. The theory assumes that, cognitively, people characterize groups by attributes that distinguish them from other groups. Ecologically, positive social information is more frequent (i.e., positivity prevalence), and negative social information is more diverse (i.e., negativity diversity). If negative attributes are less frequent and more diverse relative to positive attributes, then they must be more likely to distinguish one group from another. Consequently, the attributes people see as characteristic of a group are likely to be negative. We illustrate the predicted stereotype negativity across two studies and two existing data sets. We then formalize the theory and illustrate it with simulations showing that rare attributes can be highly diagnostic of group membership while applying to only a minority of group members. Thus, the theory explains why most stereotype content is likely negative, despite the well-documented positivity prevalence, and why stereotypes may be diagnostic and comparatively accurate, despite being descriptively inaccurate. The theory explains stereotype negativity without requiring motivational derogation, essentialist group differences, or a general negativity bias, and it clarifies when positive stereotypes should occur. We also discuss the theory's relation to dimensional models of stereotype content and consequences for interventions aimed at reducing stereotype negativity. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

10.1177/17456916261443519.title: What We Talk About When We Talk About Empathy: Toward a Common Lexicon of Empathy-Related Constructs
10.1177/17456916261443519.abstract: Almost since the term “empathy” was coined, there has been scholarly disagreement about its meaning. Today it can best be viewed as an umbrella term encompassing a host of more specific constructs, almost all of which are regularly referred to as “empathy” in some form or fashion. Promiscuous use of this global label to denote very different constructs has impaired communication among and between scholars, practitioners, and the general public. A team of 15 empathy scholars assessed this issue and created a lexicon for these specific lower-order constructs. In this article we report the result of this effort. The lower-order constructs making up this lexicon are vicarious affect , emotional contagion , emotion co-sharing , sympathy / compassion , personal distress , perspective taking , accurate inference , mimicry , synchrony , projection , and transportation . We recommend that this more specific language be used more frequently and that the umbrella term “empathy” be used more sparingly.

10.1037/apl0001433.title: When the market moves: How stock market fluctuations shape risk-related behaviors at work.
10.1037/apl0001433.abstract: How employees' personal stock holdings perform during the day has become increasingly visible and accessible, yet research has rarely examined how fluctuations in those holdings shape employees' experiences at work. Integrating cross-domain spillover and regulatory focus theories, we propose that morning fluctuation in personal stock holdings spills over into the workplace by influencing employees' risk propensity-their willingness to take or avoid risks-and, in turn, their risk-related workplace behaviors. Specifically, drawing from regulatory focus theory, we propose that a more positive (vs. negative) fluctuation in personal stock holdings than usual is associated with subsequent increases (vs. decreases) in employees' willingness to engage in risk. In a 10-day experience sampling study of full-time employees who personally invest in the South Korean stock market, a more positive morning fluctuation in stock holding value than they typically experience predicted higher state risk propensity, which subsequently led to greater risk-taking behavior and voice. These indirect effects were moderated by long-term orientation, such that employees lower (vs. higher) in long-term orientation showed greater sensitivity to morning fluctuation in stock holding value. We then conducted two complementary experiments that supported the theorized regulatory focus mechanism by demonstrating that more positive fluctuation in personal stock holdings elicited promotion focus, whereas more negative fluctuation heightened prevention focus, and that these motivational states subsequently shaped employees' willingness to engage in risk. Together, these findings highlight employees' personal stock holdings as an overlooked source of daily behavioral variability at work. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

10.1016/j.copsyc.2026.102465.title: When and why women ask (or do not): Taking stock of research on gender differences in negotiation propensity, behavior, and outcomes
10.1016/j.copsyc.2026.102465.abstract: Evidence first emerged several decades ago that women are less likely than men to initiate negotiations and perform less competitively than men in negotiations. Researchers also have discovered moderators of these effects, including structural ambiguity, representation role, and gender salience and relevance. Furthermore, the anticipation of backlash has emerged as a potential mechanism to explain gender differences in negotiations. Yet, more recent research has revealed varied findings concerning whether gender differences, underlying mechanisms, and moderators have shifted, as well as the role of intersectionality. We review the research in this area and find that the nature of gender differences in negotiation is complex, with some recent research replicating certain past findings (e.g., gender gaps in negotiation behavior) but not others (i.e., gender gaps in negotiation propensity or moderation by representation role). Still other recent research has even revealed a reversal of gender gaps in negotiation propensity, with women being more likely than men to negotiate in certain cases, and that female negotiation counterparts are liked more than male negotiation counterparts, leading to greater counterpart satisfaction. We also consider the role of statistical power given the small-to medium-sized effects typically reported: Sample size may be another important reason for inconsistent findings in the gender and negotiation literature. Finally, we consider the potential for changing gender roles. Overall, we conclude that gender differences in negotiation performance outcomes persist and are influenced by situational nuances, but that these differences have been mitigated for propensity to initiate negotiations.

10.1146/annurev-psych-021726-103815.title: Revisiting the Queen Bee Phenomenon: Understanding Self–Group Distancing in Women and Other Groups as Strategic Compliance Within Unequal Systems
10.1146/annurev-psych-021726-103815.abstract: The Queen Bee phenomenon (QBP), whereby senior women in male-dominated contexts distance themselves from junior women, align with masculine norms, and downplay gender inequality, has sparked considerable debate. This contribution reviews evidence for the QBP and argues that it reflects a way of coping with gendered organizational contexts and constrained advancement opportunities that elicit social identity threat and related motives. This contribution provides a multilevel synthesis of the consequences of QBP for individuals, their colleagues, marginalized groups, and organizations. The QBP is conceptualized as a socially embedded, context-dependent, self-reinforcing feedback loop: coping responses that may yield short-term individual benefits but undermine solidarity, legitimize inequality, and reduce pressure for structural change. Integrating insights from psychology, organizational behavior, sociology, and critical diversity research, the QBP is situated alongside related coping strategies, including code-switching, identity bifurcation, and assimilation. These dynamics point to the importance of fixing systems rather than individuals, highlighting implications for research and organizational change.

10.1111/peps.70047.title: Leaving on a High or Low Note? An Achievement Goal Perspective on Executive Retirement
10.1111/peps.70047.abstract: Executive retirement represents a pivotal career transition with significant implications. However, our understanding of the antecedents of executive retirement remains limited. We contend that, different from the retirement of general employees, it is important to position executive retirement within an achievement context and consider factors such as firm performance and achievement goal orientations. Drawing on late adulthood developmental psychology, we propose an achievement goal framework to theorize the relationship between firm performance and executive retirement, and the moderating roles of goal orientations. We theorize that firm performance is associated with two distinct mechanisms: the legacy fulfillment mechanism (salient for executives with high performance) and the selective prioritization mechanism (salient for executives with low performance), which together result in a U‐shaped relationship between firm performance and the likelihood of executive retirement. We further consider executives’ goal orientations as boundary conditions to probe the underlying mechanisms. We found general support for our theory using an archival dataset of 1840 chief executive officers from S&P 1500 firms (Study 1) and a two‐wave survey of 363 executives (Study 2). By integrating developmental psychology theories into the executive retirement literature, our research sheds light on executive retirement decisions through a developmental psychology lens.

10.1016/j.leaqua.2026.102004.title: Psychological Reactions to Subordinates’ LLM Use at Work

10.1007/s10508-026-03575-2.title: Sex Education in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Qualitative Analysis of ChatGPT-3.5 Responses to Adolescents’ Questions on Romantic Relationships and Sexuality
10.1007/s10508-026-03575-2.abstract: Large language model chatbots, such as ChatGPT, have garnered increasing attention in the field of education, due to its versatility, processing speed, and widespread accessibility. However, its application to sexual education remains understudied, highlighting the need for more research into its potential to support informed decision-making among youth. The current study aimed to document ChatGPT-3.5 responses to adolescents' questions about romantic relationships and sexuality, using a more-than-human netnography approach. To obtain these responses, 393 anonymized emails written in French and English from adolescents aged 14 to 16 were collected from a recognized youth support organization. Data were obtained through ChatGPT-3.5 from January 14 to 31, 2024. The analyses focused on identifying content violations and describing the response formats, followed by a conventional content analysis of ChatGPT-3.5 recommendations. Overall, 17.8% of the emails were flagged as potentially violating ChatGPT-3.5's content policy. Responses were provided in two formats: (1) structured text or (2) continuous text that both included an introduction clarifying the question, normalizing the experience, and/or validating emotions; a list of recommendations; and a conclusion promoting support seeking, and/or a positive outlook. The recommendations aimed to encourage adolescents to embrace authenticity and personal agency, practice self-care and build self-confidence, engage in open communication, develop meaningful relationships, and seek support when needed. The findings highlight ChatGPT's potential to contribute to comprehensive sex education for adolescents seeking information.

10.1007/s10508-026-03594-z.title: Generative AI vs. Human Sources for Sexual Health Information: Credibility, Trust, and Behavioral Intentions in a U.S. College Sample
10.1007/s10508-026-03594-z.abstract: Limited access to comprehensive sexual health education has prompted a need to consider the utility of alternative strategies, such as generative artificial intelligence (genAI), for delivering accurate and accessible sexual health information. Although genAI tools can generate health information, less is known about how perceptions of the source of information shape evaluations of content (e.g., human vs. genAI). The present study examined whether college students' perceptions of sexual health information differed based on source attribution. Participants (N = 266) were students recruited from a single university in the southeastern USA in 2025. They were randomly assigned to conditions in which they were made to believe that three sexual health passages that were identical across conditions (sexual communication, body image, and sexual pleasure and safety) were written by genAI, an academic expert, a community health professional, or a peer/social media influencer. Across outcomes-including perceived accuracy and clarity, warmth and helpfulness, trustworthiness, self-efficacy, and willingness to act-genAI-attributed information was evaluated less favorably than identical information attributed to human sources. For willingness to act, there were differences in source effects across topics, such that effects were strongest for sexual pleasure/safety and weakest for sexual communication. Findings remained significant after controlling for genAI familiarity/use and attitudes. Findings indicate that evaluations of sexual health information depend not only on informational content but also on perceived source legitimacy, suggesting that AI-based tools may be the most effective when paired with human guidance to support trust and actionability.

10.1080/00224499.2026.2736663.title: Use of Post-Coital Strategies to Prevent Pregnancy: Findings from a National Sample of Adolescents and Young Adults in the United States
10.1080/00224499.2026.2736663.abstract: In the context of increasing restrictions on sexual and reproductive health care, inadequate sex education, and increasing antihormonal contraceptive sentiment, we examined post-coital pregnancy prevention behavior among a nationally representative sample of U.S. adolescents and young adults (AYA). We developed a novel measure of post-coital contraceptive strategies (i.e., actions taken after sexual intercourse with the intent of reducing the likelihood of pregnancy) and fielded this measure for the first time as part of a 2025 online, population-based survey of English-speaking 15-29-year-olds assigned female at birth ( n = 1,259). Of the 633 AYA who reported having ever had penile-vaginal sex and were not currently pregnant, 25.0% used at least one post-coital strategy to prevent pregnancy the last time they had sex. While methods with established effectiveness (i.e., emergency contraception and copper intrauterine device) were used by 8.9% respondents, 16.1% reported using a non-medically evidenced post-coital strategy, the most common being praying (9.4%). Post-coital strategy use varied by age, race and ethnicity, and number of contraceptive methods used. In multivariable analyses, contraceptive knowledge was negatively associated with post-coital strategy use. Regardless of effectiveness, post-coital strategies are common enough to warrant inclusion in behavioral surveillance and attention in health education and clinical practice.

10.1007/s10508-026-03544-9.title: Problematic Pornography Use Among Swedish Adolescents: Characteristics and Clinical Implications
10.1007/s10508-026-03544-9.abstract: Problematic pornography use (PPU) is the most common manifestation of compulsive sexual behavior disorder (CSBD). Many adults seeking help for CSBD report onset during adolescence, yet there is limited knowledge of PPU in adolescents and its predisposing factors. This study investigated the prevalence of self-perceived PPU among Swedish adolescents and explored associated factors as well as pornography use patterns. In this cross-sectional study, data were collected from a representative sample of 3106 Swedish third-year senior high school students. Information on sociodemographic background, pornography use, sexual behaviors, health, and experiences of abuse was collected. PPU was based on self-reported difficulties in refraining from or stopping pornography use. Gender-stratified descriptive statistics and logistic regression analyses were used to examine relationships between groups and variables. PPU was reported by 10.4% of respondents, with a higher prevalence among boys (18.8%) compared to girls (3.9%). It was associated with increased time spent on pornography and higher exposure to violent or other concerning sexual content. Compared to the reference group, adolescents with PPU exhibited higher rates of abusive experiences, mental health issues, risky behaviors, and nonsuicidal self-injury. Gender-specific patterns emerged. PPU is a significant issue among Swedish adolescents, particularly boys. Addressing concerns related to pornography use, underlying vulnerabilities and gender-specific factors is crucial to prevent the progression of PPU into adulthood and in treatment efforts.

10.1080/0092623x.2026.2740624.title: “It’s Like You’re Trying to Defuse a Bomb”: Fear, Responsibility, and Shame in Young Men’s Sexual Lives
10.1080/0092623x.2026.2740624.abstract: This study examines how this generation of young heterosexual men-who have come of age in the "age of consent"-emotionally experience sex. We thematically analyzed 31 in-depth interviews with men aged 18 to 32 years. The most striking finding is how rarely these men described enjoying sex. Three themes emerged. First, anxiety and vigilance accompanied sexual encounters. Second, there was a moral concern about causing harm to a sexual partner. Third, shame arose not only from accusations by others, but also from self-criticism. The themes overlap substantially, suggesting aspects of a complex, sometimes contradictory experience. The defining feature is an inward turn: a cultural suspicion of men appears to have been internalized by some young men. For these men, the question when navigating consent is often not only "does she want this?" but "am I the kind of man who could get this wrong?" Sex, as one participant put it, is "like you're trying to defuse a bomb." These young men have come to approach sex as a hazard to manage rather than a relational experience to share. They attributed this wariness to the cultural climate that surrounds consent. We consider implications for consent education, clinical practice, and future research.

10.1007/s10508-026-03527-w.title: Facial Asymmetry and Sexuality in Women
10.1007/s10508-026-03527-w.abstract: People perceive more symmetrical individuals as more attractive; therefore, facial symmetry has been linked to mate selection. Being perceived as more attractive could also increase women's indirect reproductive benefits that would follow from pronounced sexuality and enhanced mating. Sexuality can be examined either as long-term, through sociosexual orientation, or through current sexual activity and desire. This study explored the relationship between facial asymmetry and female sexuality, while taking into account a relationship status and, due to the potential differences in facial asymmetry between female from rural and urban areas, the place of residence. Long-term sexuality was measured with the three subscales of the Sociosexual Orientation Inventory (SOI-R): Behavior, Attitude, and Desire. Current sexual activity and desire were assessed with questions about their frequency and intensity (based on the Female Sexual Function Index). Simple correlations revealed a weak, negative association between facial asymmetry and the number of sexual partners in the last year (ρ = - .23, 95% CI [- 0.45, 0.01], p = .047), SOI Attitude (ρ = - .25, 95% CI [- 0.44, - 0.03], p = .031), and sexual desire (ρ = - .21, 95% CI [- 0.43, - 0,00], p = .082). However, these effects were no longer significant after including place of residence as a confounder (.42 < p < .91). These results highlight the importance of external conditions when investigating correlates of facial asymmetry.

10.1007/s10508-026-03584-1.title: Who Is Using Pornography Generated by Artificial Intelligence? Correlates of AI-Porn Use and Familiarity in an Australian Adult Sample
10.1007/s10508-026-03584-1.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are rapidly transforming how people create and experience sexual content, including the emergence of AI-generated pornography (AI-porn). Yet little is known about who is engaging with this evolving medium. This study presents findings from a cross-sectional survey (data collected in 2025) of 367 heterosexual Australian adults (age range = 19–87 years, M = 39.07, SD = 13.43; 52.5% men, 44.8% women [and 2.2% non-binary, excluded from inferential analyses due to small cell sizes]) examining demographic, ideological, and relational correlates of AI-porn familiarity and use. Overall, 26.0% of participants reported having used AI-porn and were moderately familiar with it. Regression analyses showed that men and younger participants were significantly more likely to be familiar with and to have used AI-porn. Ideological factors (religiosity, political orientation) and relational factors (relationship status, relationship and sexual satisfaction) were not associated with use. These findings suggest that engagement with AI-porn is emerging most prominently among digitally curious younger men, yet appears ideologically broad and not linked (in this data set) to relationship dissatisfaction. As AI tools enable new forms of personalized, creative sexual expression, understanding who is exploring these technologies can help researchers and clinicians track evolving norms around intimacy, fantasy, and sexual media in the digital age.

10.1080/00224499.2026.2731571.title: Beyond Asexuality as a Single Category: Sexuality-Related Profiles and Differential Perceived Stigma-Related Impairment Across the Ace Spectrum
10.1080/00224499.2026.2731571.abstract: Asexuality is increasingly understood as a heterogeneous spectrum, yet research has rarely examined how multiple sexuality-related dimensions cluster within ace-spectrum (i.e. asexual-spectrum) populations or how such configurations relate to perceived stigma-related impairment. Using data from the 2021 Ace Community Survey (analytic N = 11,063), this study adopted a multidimensional, person-centered approach to identify sexuality-related profiles based on sexual attraction frequency, desire to act on attraction, sex drive/libido, and sex disposition. Latent profile analysis (LPA) identified four profiles: Sex-Averse Low-Attraction, Context-Dependent Low-Attraction, Higher-Frequency, and Sex-Favorable High-Attraction. The Bolck-Croon-Hagenaars approach was used to compare these profiles on a global index of perceived asexuality-related impairment and four domain-specific outcomes: harm to family relationships, socioeconomic disadvantage, social exclusion, and mental/physical health impairment. Although overall impairment levels were low, the Higher-Frequency profile showed comparatively greater perceived impairment across domains. The Sex-Averse Low-Attraction and Sex-Favorable High-Attraction profiles generally showed lower perceived impairment and did not differ from each other, except for socioeconomic disadvantage, for which the Sex-Favorable High-Attraction profile showed comparatively elevated scores. The Context-Dependent Low-Attraction profile typically fell between these groups. These findings indicate that ace-spectrum sexuality is internally heterogeneous and that sexuality-related configurations are associated with distinct patterns of perceived stigma-related impairment. By documenting within-spectrum differences, this study advances a more differentiated understanding of asexuality, minority stress, and sexuality-related vulnerability.

10.1007/s10508-026-03549-4.title: “Very Safety-Conscious and Consent-Focused”: Exploring Harm Reduction Practices at Group Sex Events
10.1007/s10508-026-03549-4.abstract: Group sex, which encompasses sexual activity among more than two people, is prevalent across diverse genders and sexualities. For many of its participants, group sex is an important source of pleasure and belonging. However, it is most often studied in the context of STI risk and related harm reduction, which isolates STI-related harm reduction behaviors from broader community norms and culture, obscuring important community dynamics. In the present study, we investigated a broad range of harm reduction practices employed by group sex participants in southwestern British Columbia, Canada. Through thematic analysis of interviews with 20 participants, we identified diverse harm reduction strategies enacted before, during, and after events to mitigate physical, emotional, and social risks. These strategies included vetting attendees in advance, establishing consent norms (e.g., consent circles, color-coded bracelets), promoting STI prevention (e.g., regular testing, barrier usage), and maintaining privacy. Findings highlight a collaborative approach to harm reduction, emphasizing both community trust and individual responsibility/accountability, reflecting a broader culture of care. This work broadens the scope of harm reduction in group sex contexts beyond STI prevention, offering insights applicable to broader sexual wellness initiatives and discussions of consent and safety in sexual communities.

10.1080/0092623x.2026.2751549.title: Digital Masculinity and Digital Media Exposure in Relation to Male Genital Self-Image, Mental Health, and Sexual Health: A Scoping Review
10.1080/0092623x.2026.2751549.abstract: ABSTARCTMale genital self-image is increasingly recognized as an important determinant of men's sexual health, psychological well-being, and body image. The rapid expansion of social media, pornography, and digital masculinity ideals has raised concerns about their influence on unrealistic genital appearance expectations; however, evidence remains fragmented across disciplines. This scoping review mapped the literature on the relationships among digital masculinity, digital media exposure, male genital self-image, psychological well-being, and sexual health. The review followed the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). Electronic databases were systematically searched without publication year restrictions, and 27 studies met the eligibility criteria. Five major themes emerged: development and psychometric evaluation of male genital self-image measures, sociocultural and digital media influences, psychological correlates, sexual health outcomes, and penile dysmorphic concerns with related interventions. Overall, lower male genital self-image was associated with higher anxiety, depressive symptoms, social appearance anxiety, body dissatisfaction, and poorer sexual functioning. Social media, pornography, and masculinity norms appeared to reinforce unrealistic genital appearance ideals, although evidence regarding the direct effects of pornography remained inconsistent. Current evidence is dominated by cross-sectional studies from high-income countries, highlighting the need for longitudinal, cross-cultural, and intervention-based research to strengthen evidence and inform clinical practice.

10.1080/0092623x.2026.2744710.title: Dyadic Associations between Body Appreciation and Sexual Function among Cisgender Heterosexual and Gender and Sexually Diverse Couples
10.1080/0092623x.2026.2744710.abstract: Given the body's exposure during partnered sexual activity, having a positive perception of one's body may impact sexual function, i.e., the capacity to respond sexually. Yet research on the associations between body appreciation and sexual function within couples is limited, particularly among couples who identify as gender and sexually diverse, who face greater risks of experiencing sexual difficulties due to minority stress. Examining body appreciation among couples may lead to clearer insights into their sexual function. The present study assessed dyadic associations between body appreciation and sexual function, examining the moderating effects of gender identity and sexual orientation, in a diverse sample of 151 couples. Results based on the actor-partner interdependence moderation model showed that a person's body appreciation was negatively related to their own sexual function difficulties, and to their partner's difficulties when the latter was heterosexual. Gender identity did not significantly moderate these associations. This study demonstrates the associations between a person's body appreciation and their own sexual function, as well as the role of the partner's sexual orientation in the association between a person's body appreciation and their partner's sexual function, highlighting the importance of considering sexual orientation to understand dyadic associations with sexual health.

10.1080/0092623x.2026.2736685.title: Sexual Distress, Concerns About Sex Life, and Successful Sexual Aging: An Exploration in Older Partnered German Adults
10.1080/0092623x.2026.2736685.abstract: Although research on older adults' sexual functioning and sexual health has increased in recent decades, there is a lack of systematic assessments of the role of sexual distress in positive sexual aging. This study examined associations between sexual distress, concerns about sex life, and positive sexual aging, and whether these associations differ by gender. Data were drawn from a 2024 online survey of partnered, sexually active German adults aged 65 years and older ( n = 598). Positive sexual aging was assessed using the Successful Sexual Aging Scale (SSAS). Structural equation modeling controlling for age showed that distress about sexual functioning was strongly and negatively associated with successful sexual aging in both women and men. Concerns about sex life were additionally and uniquely associated with lower SSAS scores among women. Findings underscore the importance of assessing sexual distress and gender-specific concerns in older adults' sexual health care.

10.1080/00224499.2026.2743644.title: Mediators and Moderators of Treatment Outcome Following Online Mindfulness and Cognitive-Behavioral Treatment for Female Sexual Interest/Arousal Disorder
10.1080/00224499.2026.2743644.abstract: eSense is a digital tool delivering mindfulness-based therapy (MBT) and cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) to individuals with female sexual interest/arousal disorder (SIAD). eSense is feasible, usable, satisfying, and efficacious, and helps overcome barriers to care. We sought to examine potential mediators and moderators of improvements in sexual desire and distress following use of eSense . Women with SIAD ( n = 129, mean age 44.8 ± 12.3 in the MBT arm and 41.9 ± 13.1 in the CBT arm) were randomly assigned to arm and completed self-report measures at baseline, mid-treatment, immediately post-treatment, and 6-month follow-up. Potential mediators were changes in depression, posttraumatic stress disorder symptoms (PTSD), and avoidance of sexual activity. We examined treatment expectations after module 1 as a potential moderator, and partner involvement, homework completion, and modules completed as process indicators that may predict magnitude of improvement. Decreases in depressive and PTSD symptoms were associated with improvements in sexual desire and distress in the MBT arm, and reductions in sexual avoidance were associated with improvements in both arms. Higher expectations for treatment were associated with greater improvements in desire and distress for those in the CBT arm only, whereas partner involvement, homework completion, and number of eSense modules completed were associated with improvements in both arms. This study helps identify putative mechanisms by which digital health tools for SIAD, like eSense , may be effective, and to identify participant characteristics as well as treatment engagement factors that might be associated with differential responses to online MBT and CBT.

10.1007/s10508-026-03551-w.title: Social Media Use and Openness to “Sugar Relationships”: Cultural Tightness–Looseness as a Moderator Across 22 Countries
10.1007/s10508-026-03551-w.abstract: Social media use has been widely linked to sexual attitudes, yet it remains unclear whether its association with openness to sugar relationships is uniform across countries or contingent on country-level normative contexts. In the present study, we examined whether country-level cultural tightness–looseness moderated the relationship between social media use and openness to sugar relationships across 22 countries. Openness to sugar relationships was conceptualized as a manifestation of a broader orientation toward sexual–economic exchange. Using data from 22,292 adult women drawn from a large cross-national dataset, we tested this framework with Bayesian multilevel modeling. Measurement invariance of the openness construct was assessed, and alignment procedures were applied to address cross-country non-invariance prior to analysis. Cultural tightness–looseness was modeled as a country-level moderator of the individual-level association between social media use and openness to sugar relationships, while age was included as a control variable. Results revealed a positive association between social media use and openness to sugar relationships. In addition, this association was modestly stronger in countries characterized by lower normative constraint, suggesting that country-level norm strength may shape the attitudinal relevance of digital exposure. Models including this interaction outperformed alternative specifications that incorporated a range of theoretically plausible country-level covariates, including indicators of digital infrastructure, socioeconomic structure, and internet freedom. Although the interaction effect size was modest, the findings suggest that the attitudinal correlates of social media use vary systematically across countries and highlight the importance of country-level normative contexts in research on sexual–economic openness.

10.1007/s10508-026-03542-x.title: Why Do Spanish University Students Flirt in Nightlife Venues?
10.1007/s10508-026-03542-x.abstract: Recent years have seen increased scientific interest in sexual behaviors in nightlife settings. The majority of studies focus on criminal behaviors, such as sexual harassment and violence. The present study, by contrast, examined practices of flirtation among Spanish university students in nightlife settings with the primary aim of understanding why these practices are undertaken. The data come from nine focus-group interviews and 20 individual interviews. The results showed that flirtation served multiple purposes beyond mere playfulness or expressions of interest. The most salient of these were: seeking immediate pleasure; hooking up; working through current or former relationships; and acquiring sexual capital. This research advances understanding of the complicated art of flirtation, which is an activity highly valued among students, yet also potentially precarious and, at times, a source of harm.

10.1007/s10508-026-03545-8.title: Distraction and Desire: Extending the Study of Non-Erotic Thoughts to the South Asian Context
10.1007/s10508-026-03545-8.abstract: Non-erotic thoughts (NETs) are intrusive cognitions that interfere with sexual enjoyment and have been linked to sexual dysfunction. Despite recognition that sexuality is culturally rooted, no research has examined whether NETs vary across cultures. We investigated cultural differences in NET frequency, anxiety, and content between South Asian and White women in Canada, the USA, and the UK. Given South Asian sexual norms emphasizing procreative sex within marriage and potential guilt/shame when transgressed, we predicted group differences in culturally relevant NET categories. We recruited two independent samples of White women and second-generation South Asian women via Prolific (Sample 1 N = 301; Sample 2 N = 284). Participants completed a modified version of Purdon and Holdaway's (2006) NET measure assessing frequency and associated anxiety. Independent-samples t tests revealed that overall NET frequency and anxiety did not differ significantly between groups. However, two thought categories showed robust cultural differences across both samples: morality/guilt/regret and pregnancy/STI/health concerns. South Asian women reported both higher frequency and higher anxiety for these categories, with effect sizes in the small-to-moderate range (d = .24-.53). Sample 2 revealed additional category-level differences.
