These findings demonstrate that cultural influences on NETs are domain-specific rather than global, with the largest effects emerging for morality/guilt thoughts, consistent with cultural norms emphasizing sexual modesty. Findings underscore the need for culturally sensitive sexuality models and therapeutic approaches.

10.1007/s10508-026-03538-7.title: Together and Apart: Dual Attachment Bonds to Cohabiting and Separated Partners Predict Relationship and Psychological Outcomes During COVID-19 Lockdowns
10.1007/s10508-026-03538-7.abstract: During the COVID-19 pandemic, many people relied on romantic partners for support despite physical separation. This study expands the concept of a safe haven by examining how multi-partner attachment systems influenced intrapersonal (e.g., mental health) and interpersonal (e.g., relationship satisfaction, commitment) outcomes among people in at least two concurrent committed relationships during the COVID-19 pandemic. Specifically, 186 people practicing polyamory who were separated from one partner(s) and cohabiting with another partner(s) completed a survey during March to May of 2020. Analyses indicated that attachment anxiety and avoidance negatively predicted relationship satisfaction within each relationship with cohabiting and SPs. Attachment anxiety to both cohabiting and separated partners further predicted greater COVID distress. Attachment avoidance to a cohabiting partner negatively predicted COVID distress while attachment avoidance to a separated partner positively predicted COVID distress. One unique cross-relationship effect emerged: attachment anxiety to a separated partner predicted increased commitment to a cohabiting partner.

10.1007/s10508-026-03540-z.title: Being a Partner or a Mother: Breastfeeding Mothers’ Perceptions and Experiences of Breast Milk and Sexuality in the Postpartum Period
10.1007/s10508-026-03540-z.abstract: This study aimed to explore breastfeeding mothers’ perceptions and experiences related to breast milk and sexuality between the third and sixth months postpartum. A descriptive qualitative design was employed. The sample consisted of 10 mothers, including primiparous ( n = 4) and multiparous ( n = 6) women, with a mean age of 29 years. Data were collected through individual semi-structured interviews. Thematic analysis was used to analyze the data. Three main themes emerged from the analysis: avoidance of sexuality, maintaining sexuality as a responsibility, and coping with the effects of breastfeeding on sexuality. Six subthemes were identified within these main themes: physical changes in sexual dynamics; psychological changes in sexual dynamics; religious, social, and cultural influences on sexuality; fulfillment of the female role; changing perceptions of breasts; and various coping strategies. The findings suggest that breastfeeding and postpartum physiological and sociocultural factors shape mothers’ sexual experiences, with sexuality often being perceived as inappropriate during this period due to cultural and religious norms, while participants’ perceptions related to breast milk also contribute to these experiences. Mothers attempt to balance breastfeeding with maintaining their sexual relationships, which frequently leads to emotional distress. It is recommended that healthcare professionals address breastfeeding, breast milk, and sexuality within breastfeeding education programs and provide individualized, culturally sensitive guidance for couples.

10.1080/0092623x.2026.2741355.title: Moving Beyond a Binary Cis-Heteronormative Perspective: A Scoping Review of Instruments for Inclusive Research into Sexual Functioning
10.1080/0092623x.2026.2741355.abstract: Cis- and heteronormativity hinder the valid measurement of sexual function in Sexual Orientation and Gender Diversity (SOGD) populations. This study aimed to identify instruments designed for inclusive use and to evaluate their cross-cultural and psychometric characteristics. A scoping review was conducted by searching PubMed, EBSCOhost, and Web of Science in April 2026. The search terms included sexual function, gender, sexual orientation, assessment instruments, and psychometric information. Screening, data extraction, and quality grading were performed independently by two reviewers. Fifteen articles described the development or validation of instruments for use among SOGD populations. Notably, non-binary individuals were included in only one study. For most instruments, adequate content and structural validity, and internal consistency were reported, but evidence for cross-gender, cross-sexual orientation, cross-cultural, criterion, and construct validity was lacking or unclear. Limited or no information was provided on test-retest reliability, measurement error, and responsiveness to changes in sexual function for the instruments used. Most identified instruments were validated in narrowly defined subgroups or assessed only a single domain of sexual functioning, limiting their suitability as general, SOGD-inclusive measures. This review supports the need to develop and validate new inclusive instruments to measure sexual function, including SOGD populations.

10.1007/s10508-026-03548-5.title: “There’s No Magic Pill to Help Me, Right?”: Sex After Early Midlife Bilateral Salpingo-Oophorectomy
10.1007/s10508-026-03548-5.abstract: Women with risk-reducing bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (RRBSO) report poorer sexual health than women of a similar age with intact ovaries. Since women with RRBSO lose the ability to make endogenous 17-β-estradiol (E2), open questions include whether: (1) poorer sexual function is associated with E2 loss and (2) exogenous estradiol therapy (ET BSO ) is related to amelioration of objective decrements and subjective experiences. We combined online questionnaires with qualitative interviews to explore the sexual function of women with pathogenic variants in the BRCA1/2 genes and RRBSO not taking ET BSO (RRBSO) and those taking ET BSO (RRBSO + ET BSO ). We compared their quantitative responses to those of age-matched women with intact ovaries (AMC) and women in spontaneous menopause (SM). RRBSO had lower total sexual function scores than AMC and more sexually related distress than AMC than SM. In terms of lived experience with RRBSO + /–ET BSO , qualitative interviews mirrored the quantitative data with reports of pain, loss of sexual desire, and dryness, in addition to concerns about identity, relational challenges, and lacking crucial information regarding sexual response after RRBSO. The combination of the objective and subjective reports details worse sexual function and experience of younger women with RRBSO regardless of ET BSO . Since ET BSO does not appear to ameliorate all aspects of sexual function and distress for many women with RRBSO, it is critical to consider other interventions including fully informed consent prior to RRBSO.

10.1007/s10508-026-03659-z.title: Cohort Change in Attitudes About Adolescent Gender Transitions Between 2018 and 2025
10.1007/s10508-026-03659-z.abstract: Medical gender transition for adolescents who identify as transgender is a contentious topic. The previous research evaluated data from respondents interviewed in 2018 and examined predictors of support for adolescent hormonal and surgical transitioning. Nevertheless, much has changed in public debates since that time. The present study evaluates data from a 2025 nationally representative survey which fielded a series of questions identical to those posed in 2018 in order to examine changes in attitudes among English-speaking American adults about gender dysphoric adolescents medically transitioning for the purpose of gender affirmation. Results indicate significant decreases in support between 2018 and 2025 for such medical transitioning. We examine cross-sectional, period changes, and changes within birth cohorts. Significant increases in disagreement with medical transitioning appear for all age cohorts born in 1988 or earlier. Given this changing landscape, we reexamine predictors of support for adolescent medical transition.

10.1007/s10508-026-03669-x.title: Detransition, Posttraumatic Stress Disorder, and Moral Injury
10.1007/s10508-026-03669-x.abstract: There are increasing reports of individuals who, after undergoing medical gender-affirming treatments (GAT) for gender incongruence/gender dysphoria, subsequently detransition and/or express regret regarding these interventions. Although detransition experiences are heterogeneous, some individuals who detransition describe substantial adverse physical consequences and psychological distress resulting from the GAT they received. The purpose of this article is to assist mental health professionals in their understanding and conceptualizing of detransition experiences within the existing Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) framework. It is posited that a diagnosis of posttraumatic stress disorder, as delineated in the most recent text revision of the DSM (DSM-5-TR) (American Psychiatric Association, 2022), may be applicable for some individuals who have detransitioned. Furthermore, the relevance of the moral injury concept-recently incorporated into the DSM-5-TR under code Z65.8 (American Psychiatric Association, 2025)-as it pertains to this population, is discussed.

10.1080/00224499.2026.2733985.title: In Harm’s Way: How the 2024 U.S. Election Might Affect Sexual- and Gender-Minority Health
10.1080/00224499.2026.2733985.abstract: Immediately after taking office in 2025, the current U.S. presidential administration established an unprecedented number of policies hostile to sexual- and gender-minority (SGM) populations: restricting the rights and social legitimacy of transgender individuals, curtailing youth access to gender-affirming medical care, terminating federal research and data collection on sexual and gender diversity, and restricting open discussion of sexual and gender diversity in educational settings. These events pose a greater threat to SGM health than previous state-level hostile policies, because of their scope, speed, and scale, and because they serve to institutionalize animus toward gender-minority populations into U.S. law and policy. We use extant research on structural stigma to predict the most likely mental and physical health consequences of these events, and we also forecast health consequences for the family members of SGM individuals and individuals whose paid employment involves SGM populations. We review evidence for the mechanisms through which these effects may unfold (institutional changes, increased minority stress, decreased social safety, and behavioral changes) and identify subpopulations at disproportionate risk (gender-minority populations, youth, those facing intersectional stigma, and those with existing health vulnerabilities). We conclude with a call for targeted efforts to ameliorate these negative health consequences, and we review research indicating that increasing social support and safety is the most effective and feasible strategy for doing so. We call for urgent, community-based efforts to increase the number and quality of nurturant social connections among all individuals who have been placed in harm's way by the changed U.S. political climate.
